49	\section{Automatic Widening}
50	\seclabel{widening}
51	
52	\begin{Grammar}
53	\emph{Coercion} &::=&
54	\KWD{coerce}\option{\emph{StaticParams}}\texttt(\emph{BindId} \emph{IsType}\texttt)\emph{CoercionClauses} \KWD{widens} \EXP{=} \emph{Expr}\\
55	
56	\end{Grammar}
57	
58	
59	Fortress supports what is sometimes called ``widest-need'' evaluation
60	of numerical expressions.  To see the problem, suppose that \VAR{a}
61	and \VAR{b} are 32-bit floating-point numbers and \VAR{c} is a 64-bit
62	floating-point number.  It is easy, and tempting, to write an
63	expression such as
64	%% c = c + a \cdot b
65	\begin{Fortress}
66	\(c = c + a \cdot b\)
67	\end{Fortress}
68	but if you stop to think about it, if interpreted naively it will
69	compute the product \EXP{a \cdot b} as a 32-bit floating-point number,
70	and the impression that the sum may be accurate to the precision of a
71	64-bit floating-point number is only an illusion.  Widest-need
72	processing takes context into account and ``widens'' (or ``upgrades'')
73	the operands \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} to 64-bit floating-point numbers
74	before the product is computed, so that the product will be computed
75	as a 64-bit result.
76	
77	Before widening is considered, a Fortress compiler,
78	in its normal course of operation, analyzes
79	an expression bottom-up.  For every functional invocation, it needs
80	to statically identify a specific declaration to be invoked.
81	Once this is done, then for %every argument position of
82	every functional invocation, one of two conditions holds:
83	(a) The type of the argument expression is a subtype of the
84	    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
85	(b) The type of the argument expression can be coerced to the
86	    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
87	
88	This process has to be done bottom-up because in order to select a
89	specific declaration for a functional invocation, it is necessary to
90	know the types of the argument expressions, and if an argument
91	expression is itself a functional invocation, it is necessary to
92	select the specific declaration for that invocation in order to find
93	out the return type of the invocation.
94	
95	Once an expression has been fully analyzed in this way, then widening
96	is performed as a top-down process.  For each functional invocation
97	that appears in a context where a coercion can occur, ask
98	whether the argument expression (which, remember, is a functional invocation)
99	falls under case (a) or case (b) above.  If case (b), coercion of the
100	functional result is required; if the relevant coercion declaration is
101	a ``widening'' coercion, then this functional invocation is a
102	candidate for widening.  Call the type of the functional invocation
103	\VAR{T}, and call the expected type of the coercion context, \VAR{U}.
104	
105	
106	When the functional call was considered during the bottom-up analysis,
107	in general many overloaded declarations may have been considered; of
108	all those that were applicable with coercion
109	to the static call, the most specific one was chosen.
110	When considering widening, we consider the same set of declarations, but
111	first discard all declarations whose return types are not subtypes of
112	\VAR{U}.  Then if any remain, and there is a unique most specific one
113	among them, then that declaration is attached to the functional call
114	instead.  In this way a coercion step is eliminated (coercion is no
115	longer needed to convert the result of the functional invocation from
116	type \VAR{T} to type \VAR{U}), possibly at the expense of requiring
117	a new coercion in a subexpression---but this is exactly the desired
118	effect.  Once this is done, then the subexpressions of the functional
119	call are processed recursively.
120	
121	
122	This process is general enough not only to provide for
123	widening floating-point precision, but to handle two other cases
124	of interest as well: widening point computations to interval computations,
125	and widening computations involving aggregate data structures whose
126	components are widenable.  For example, in \EXP{d (v \times w)} suppose that
127	\VAR{d} is of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and \VAR{v} and \VAR{w} are 3-vectors with components
128	of type $\mathbb{R}32$; this strategy is capable of promoting \VAR{v} and \VAR{w}
129	to 3-vectors with components of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and then performing all
130	computations with $\mathbb{R}64$ precision.
131	
132	Let's go through the example of \EXP{c + a \cdot b} in detail.
133	The relevant declarations might look something like this:
134	%trait RR32
135	%  ...
136	%end
137	%
138	%trait RR64
139	%  coerce(x:RR32) widens = ...
140	%  ...
141	%end
142	
143	%opr DOT(l: RR32, r: RR32): RR32 = ... (* 1 *)
144	%opr DOT(l: RR64, r: RR64): RR64 = ... (* 2 *)
145	%opr +(l: RR32, r: RR32): RR32 = ... (* 3 *)
146	%opr +(l: RR64, r: RR64): RR64 = ... (* 4 *)
147	\begin{Fortress}
148	\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}32\)\\
149	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
150	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
151	\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}64\)\\
152	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{R}32) \KWD{widens}\: = \ldots\)\\
153	\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
154	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
155	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  1 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
156	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  2 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
157	\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  3 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
158	\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  4 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)
159	\end{Fortress}
160	
161	The bottom-up analysis observes that \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} are both of type
162	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, and discovers that declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}
163	are both applicable to the product, but declaration \EXP{1}
164	would be chosen because it requires no coercion and declaration \EXP{2}
165	would require coercion of both arguments to type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
166	The analysis then observes that \VAR{c} has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
167	and the product expression has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, so declaration
168	\EXP{3} is not applicable but declaration \EXP{4} is applicable
169	(though requiring a coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} for its second argument).
170	
171	Now the top-down widening analysis is performed.  The product is
172	a functional call that is an argument to another functional call,
173	and its result requires coercion, and that coercion is a widening
174	coercion.  Therefore the compiler reconsiders the applicable
175	declarations, which were declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}.
176	The result type of declaration \EXP{1} is not a subtype
177	of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, but the result type of declaration \EXP{2}
178	is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (in fact, it \emph{is} \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}).
179	Declaration \EXP{2} is the most specific among the applicable declarations
180	with that property (in fact, in this example it's the only one),
181	so declaration \EXP{2} replaces declaration \EXP{1} for the
182	product invocation.  This in turn requires \VAR{a} and \VAR{b}
183	to be coerced from type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
184	before the product is performed.
185	
186	Widening is a tricky business, best left to expert library designers.
187	When used judiciously, it can greatly improve the precision of
188	numerical computations without requiring a great deal of thought on
189	the part of the application programmer and without cluttering up code
190	with explicit conversions.
191	
192	\emph{Future versions of this specification will include tables of
193	  coercions and widening coercions supported by \library.}

355	## 6. `RR32` a sibling of `RR64`
356	
357	The fork: whether anything in the library or the corpus argues for keeping `RR32` below `RR64`, against the specification, the later Types chapter, the team's 2009 commit and the compiler library (`explorations/reviews/batch-6-conformance.md`, finding 3).
358	
359	The prototype, `probes/rr32/rr32-sibling.patch`, library only: `value object RR32 extends { Number, StandardPartialOrder[\RR32\], StandardMinMax[\RR32\], AdditiveGroup[\RR32\], MultiplicativeRing[\RR32\] }`, the algebra `RR64` carries at its own type; every `b:RR64` parameter of `RR32`'s natives made `b:RR32` (row 435's second fix) and its `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX` answering `RR32`; `RR64` excluding `RR32`, no longer comprising it, and declaring `coerce(x: RR32) = asFloat(x)`, as the compiler library's `RR64` does (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:433-435`); `Number` comprising `RR32`. Three library sites needed more on the way, each recorded in the patch:
360	- `RR32`'s `^(self, b:ZZ64):RR32`, beside `^(self, b:Number):RR64`, broke the return-type rule once `RR32` is no longer an `RR64`, and so did `MultiplicativeRing`'s `^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T` beside the `Number` form; the prototype gives `RR32` one `^(self, b:AnyIntegral):RR32` on its own native and drops the other two integer forms.
361	- `Number`'s `=` compares a float with any number after `asFloat`, but tests for a float by `typecase ... RR64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:358-365`); the prototype adds the `RR32` case, since an `RR32` would otherwise fall to `exactValue` and compare as 0/0.
362	
363	`RR32Micro.fss`: on the base (`RR32Micro.base.txt`) an `RR32` value is an `RR64` in a `typecase`, and `a + 2.5` ends the run with `InterpreterBug: getRR32 not implemented for FFloatLiteral` (row 435). On the prototype (`RR32Micro.sibling.txt`) the value is an `RR32` and not an `RR64`; `a + b` is an `RR32` 4.0; `a + 2.5` and `2.5 + a` are 4.0 and `a + 2` is 3.5, by `RR64`'s arithmetic after the coercion, which is the specification's worked example (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:861-898`); and an `RR32` passed to an `RR64` parameter converts.
364	
365	**What the first shape missed.** `RR32`'s api declares its getters, one `^` and `MINNUM`/`MAXNUM` only (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:47-74`); its other operators are declared in the component alone. An operator `RR32` shares with `RR64` through an algebra trait (`+`, `-`, `DOT`, `TIMES`, juxtaposition, `^`, `MIN`, `MAX`) reaches `RR32`'s own declaration through the trait's. The rest (`/`, `SQRT`, the `_UP`, `_DOWN` and `IEEE_` forms, `|self|`, `floor`, `ceiling`, `truncate` and the others) are visible to a program only as `RR64`'s functional methods, which `RR64`'s api declares (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:313-372`). On the base an `RR32` is an `RR64`, so `RR64`'s `/` dispatches on its receiver to `RR32`'s; with the first shape `a / b` converts both `RR32` operands to `RR64` and answers an `RR64` (`probes/rr32/RR32Div2.fss`, `RR32Div2.sibling.txt`: `/`, `SLASH_UP`, `PLUS_UP` and `SQRT` answer `RR64`, the other five `RR32`).
366	
367	**The second shape**, `probes/rr32/rr32-sibling-api.patch`, is the first plus 46 lines in `RR32`'s api declaring the operators its component defines, in `RR64`'s form (it applies to 2851e5086). With it all nine operators of `RR32Div2` answer `RR32` (`RR32Div2.sibling-api.txt`), and `RR32Micro` answers as with the first shape except that `SQRT a` is now `RR32`'s own, `1.2247449`, where the first shape computed it as an `RR64` (`RR32Micro.sibling-api.txt`).
368	
369	**The corpus passes.** Rung F's three passes (`count-run.sh`, one JVM per test and private caches; `compare-normalised.py`, batch 5's normalisation) over the 414 files of `ProjectFortress/tests/` at 2851e5086, their machine lines and times in `probes/rr32/passes-machine.txt`: base A (30 minutes), base B and the first shape's edit (34 minutes each, run side by side), then the second shape's edit after them.
370	- The first shape (`probes/rr32/compare-sibling.txt`): 386 the same, 7 equal once normalised (library lines the edit moved), 17 unstable (the two base passes differ: timings, random data, task traces), and 4 changed. `XXXRR32MixedRungF` passes (exit 1 to 0), row 435's expected failure, which the rung promotes. `testRR32`, a team test, fails at its line 30, `infinity: RR32 = narrow(1.0) / narrow(0.0)`, "RHS expression type Float is not assignable to LHS type RR32": the missing api declarations above. `XXXArrayLiteralArgRungC` keeps its verdict, and its message lists `RR32`'s own `-` among the candidates where it listed `RR64`'s. `XXXInheritedOverload` names its two declarations in the other order, which its row calls unstable (row 430).
371	- The second shape (`probes/rr32/compare-sibling-api.txt`; 10 minutes, the load 2.2 at its start against 10 to 13 for the others): 387 the same, 7 equal once normalised, the same 17 unstable, and 3 changed, each keeping the verdict the rung expects. `XXXRR32MixedRungF` passes (row 435's expected failure). `XXXArrayLiteralArgRungC` keeps its verdict, and its message lists `RR32`'s own `-` and `RR32`'s instance of `AdditiveGroup`'s `-` among the candidates, where it listed `RR64`'s `-` with `RR32` in its receiver's type. `XXXCoercionTupleOverloadRungC` keeps its verdict and prints its two `pair` declarations in the other order, a set's order and not a property of the program, as in row 430's message. `testRR32` passes, as on the base, and no other output changes.
372	
373	So the corpus relies on the subtype nowhere but in `RR32`'s own declarations and the three library sites above; no team test line changes.

6	
7	The one library already solves this problem the same way five times, never on an integer type:
8	
9	- `TotalComparison` declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, with exactly `StandardTotalOrder`'s bodies at its own type (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:172-175`, api `.fsi:129-131`), under the team's comment "Avoid ambiguity between the default definitions of CMP and >=" (`:161-163`). The three are the revival's, added by climb batch 7 rung H; the comment is the team's (provenance below).
10	- `RR64` (`.fss:427-429`, api `.fsi:326-328`) and `QQ` (`.fss:582-591`, api `.fsi:412-414`) declare all three at their own type, beside the ones they inherit from `StandardMinMax`.
11	- `Float` and `RR32` in `FortressBuiltin` declare them in the component only, on natives (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:93-99`, `:261-268`).
12	- Other operators of the same family use the same device. `ZZ64` declares `>`, `>=`, `<=` and `CMP` itself (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:788-794`) under the team's comment "Argh! Due to method ambiguities with ZZ, these definitions must be given explicitly here." (`:786-787`). `ZZ` declares `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP` (`:943-947`).
13	
14	Outside the one library, the same device appears three more times:
15	- The compiler library declares all three on every integer type and on `IntLiteral` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:137-139`, `:198-200`, `:261-263`, `:318-320`, `:378-380`, `:425-427`; bodies at `CompilerBuiltin.fss:552-554`, `:649-651`, `:738-740`, `:803-805`, `:869-871`). It does so on `ZZ32` although `ZZ32` also extends `StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\]` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210`).
16	- The team's unfinished draft declares `MAX` and `MIN` on `ZZ` and `QQ`, and `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM` beside them on `ZZ` (`Library/incomplete/basic/Fortress.Number.fsi:144-147`, `:43-44`).
17	- The specification's `ZZ` declares `MAX`, `MIN`, `MAXNUM` and `MINNUM`, and no `MINMAX` (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:263-266`).
18	
19	Provenance, by `git blame` at the base (`bce66f1fa`):
20	- The team's, present at the history's earliest reachable commit (`5a68404fd`, 2012-07-19): `StandardTotalOrder`'s bodies (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:285-288`), `QQ`'s own three (`:582-587`), the comment over `TotalComparison` (`:161-163`), the compiler library's declarations and bodies, the draft's and the specification's.
21	- The team's device, retyped by the revival: `RR64`'s (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:427-429`), `Float`'s and `RR32`'s (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:95-99`, `:263-268`) are declared at `Number` in `5a68404fd` and were retyped to `RR64` by climb batch 6 rung F in `d846e3644` (2026-09-27).
22	- The revival's: `TotalComparison`'s three (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:172-175`, api `.fsi:129-131`), added by climb batch 7 rung H in `952892a00` (2026-09-28).
23	
24	So the precedent followed is the team's: `StandardTotalOrder`'s bodies (`:285-288`) at the type's own type, as `QQ` declares its own three (`:582-587`) and as the compiler library declares all three on every integer type. `TotalComparison`'s three are the revival's restatement of the same device.

(** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.

trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    abstract getter one(): T
    abstract opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T

#!/bin/bash
# count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]: runs every file of <list-file> under
# `walk`, one JVM per test, and writes its output to <work-dir>/log/<test>.txt with an rc= secs= trailer.
# The shape of explorations/reviews/mie-probes/keep/nestprobe/run-tests.sh without its NestProbe shadow:
# each shard has its own FORTRESS_CACHES, so default_repository/ is never read or written and no two JVMs
# share a cache.  A shadow classes directory, if given, is put ahead of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath.
set -u
cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.."                               # $FORTRESS_HOME
# env.sh without its rm of /tmp/fortress*rats, which a parallel agent's runs may be using
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH="/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH" FORTRESS_HOME="$(pwd)" FORTRESS_THREADS=1
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
W=${1:?usage: count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]}
L=${2:?usage: count-run.sh <work-dir> <list-file> [shadow-classes-dir] [shards]}
SH=${3:-}
N=${4:-4}
mkdir -p "$W/log"
CP=$(./bin/fortress_classpath 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
[ -n "$SH" ] && CP="$SH:$CP"
# one core per JVM, as the precedent: four run at once
FAST="-XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1"
echo "start $(date -u +%FT%TZ) load: $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg) shadow: ${SH:-none}"
for i in $(seq 0 $((N-1))); do
  (
    C="$W/caches-$i"; T="$W/tmp-$i"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"
    [ -f "$C/global.map" ] || printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
    awk -v n=$N -v i=$i 'NR % n == i' "$L" | while read -r f; do
      t=$(basename "$f" .fss)
      grep -q '^rc=' "$W/log/$t.txt" 2>/dev/null && continue
      start=$(date +%s)
      FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" timeout -k 10 600 \
        java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir="$T" $FAST -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell walk "$f" \
        < /dev/null > "$W/log/$t.txt" 2>&1
      rc=$?
      printf '\nrc=%s secs=%s\n' "$rc" "$(( $(date +%s) - start ))" >> "$W/log/$t.txt"
    done
  ) &
done
wait
rm -f ProjectFortress/tests/poem.out
echo "done $(date -u +%FT%TZ): $(grep -l '^rc=' "$W"/log/*.txt | wc -l) logs"

(* RR32Micro -- plan 6.5's RR32 probe: RR32 a sibling of RR64 under Number, as the compiler
   prelude has it (CompilerBuiltin.fsi, trait RR32 and RR64's coerce(x: RR32)), RR64
   converting from RR32 by coercion, RR32's binary natives taking an RR32 (row 435's second
   fix).  The specification's worked example (conversions-coercions.tex, the RR32 and RR64
   example) computes an RR32 with an RR64 by RR64's declaration. *)
component RR32Micro
export Executable

fR(x: RR64): String = "RR64 " x

run(): () = do
  a: RR32 = narrow(1.5)
  b: RR32 = narrow(2.5)
  println("a + b = " (a + b) " is " (typecase a + b of RR32 => "an RR32"; RR64 => "an RR64"; else => "other" end))
  println("a is " (typecase a of RR64 => "an RR64"; RR32 => "an RR32"; else => "other" end))
  println("a + 2.5 = " (a + 2.5))
  println("2.5 + a = " (2.5 + a))
  println("a + 2 = " (a + 2))
  println("a = 1.5: " (a = 1.5))
  println(fR(a))
  println("sqrt a = " (SQRT a))
  println("END")
end
end

#!/bin/bash
# walk1.sh <dir> <Name> [shadow-dir]: one program under walk from an empty private cache, with an optional
# classpath shadow, captured to <dir>/<Name>.<label>.txt where label is $LABEL (default walk).
D="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "$D/env-noclean.sh"
P=$(cd "${1:?usage}" && pwd); N=${2:?usage}; SH=${3:-}; LB=${LABEL:-walk}
C="$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/c-walk1-$N-$LB"; T="$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/t-walk1-$N-$LB"
rm -rf "$C" "$T"; mkdir -p "$C" "$T"; printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map"
CP=$("$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1); [ -n "$SH" ] && CP="$SH:$CP"
cd "$P"
{ echo "# walk1.sh $N $LB $(date -u +%FT%TZ); tree $(git -C "$FORTRESS_HOME" rev-parse --short HEAD) + $(git -C "$FORTRESS_HOME" diff --stat | tail -1); nproc=$(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //') MHz; load $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | grep -m1 version); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; shadow ${SH:-none}"
  FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" timeout -k 10 900 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Djava.io.tmpdir="$T" -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell walk "$N.fss" 2>&1
  echo "rc=$?"; } > "$P/$N.$LB.txt" 2>&1
rm -rf "$C" "$T"
cat "$P/$N.$LB.txt"
#!/bin/bash
# comp.sh <dir-of-probe> <Name> [shadow-classes-dir]: compile <dir>/<Name>.fss with the bytecode compiler in the
# compiler's world into a private cache seeded from tmp/libcache, run it, and capture <dir>/<Name>.comp.txt
# (the shape of explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement/comp.sh, with env-noclean.sh and a shadow).
D="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "$D/env-noclean.sh"
JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS ${EXTRA_FLAGS:-}"
P=$(cd "${1:?usage}" && pwd); N=${2:?usage}; SH=${3:-}
L="$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/libcache"
C="$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/cache-comp-$N"
rm -rf "$C"; cp -r "$L" "$C"; mkdir -p "$C/tmp"
CP=$("$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1)
[ -n "$SH" ] && CP="$SH:$CP"
cd "$P"
{
  echo "# comp.sh $N $(date -u +%FT%TZ); tree $(git -C "$FORTRESS_HOME" rev-parse --short HEAD); nproc=$(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //') MHz; load $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | grep -m1 version); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; shadow ${SH:-none}"
  echo "## fortress compile $N.fss (private cache, compiler's world)"
  timeout -k 10 1800 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$C -Djava.io.tmpdir=$C/tmp -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile "$N.fss" 2>&1
  echo "compile rc=$?"
  echo "## run"
  timeout -k 10 600 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches="$C" -cp "$C/bytecode_cache:$C/bytecode_cache/*:$C/nativewrapper_cache:$CP" com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper "$N" 2>&1
  echo "run rc=$?"
} > "$P/$N.comp.txt" 2>&1
cat "$P/$N.comp.txt"
# env-noclean.sh: explorations/experiment/env.sh without its rm of /tmp/fortress*rats, which the
# parallel runs of batch 6b and the distance measurement may be using. Source it from $FORTRESS_HOME.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=${FORTRESS_THREADS:-1}
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8"

# libcache.sh <dir>: the compiled path's library cache, built once in library order into <dir>
# (the shape of explorations/reviews/flattening-questions-ways/libcache.sh, with env-noclean.sh).
D="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "$D/env-noclean.sh"
L=${1:?usage: libcache.sh <dir>}
rm -rf "$L"; mkdir -p "$L/tmp"
cd "$FORTRESS_HOME"
for f in ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
         Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss Library/CompilerLibrary.fss Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do

    JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$L -Djava.io.tmpdir=$L/tmp" timeout -k 10 1800 bin/fortress compile "$f" || exit 1

component testRR32
export Executable

run():() = do
  x : RR32 = narrow(14.0)
  y : RR32 = narrow(14.0)
  z : RR32 = x y
  v : RR32 = narrow(4.5)
  w : RR32 = narrow(-4.5)
  sum : RR32 = narrow(28.0)
  mul : RR32 = narrow(196.0)
  zero : RR32 = narrow(0.0)
  one : RR32 = narrow(1.0)
  two : RR32 = narrow(2.0)
  four : RR32 = narrow(4.0)
  five : RR32 = narrow(5.0)
  nfour : RR32 = narrow(-4.0)
  nfive : RR32 = narrow(-5.0)
  infinity: RR32 = narrow(1.0) / narrow(0.0)
  NaN: RR32 = infinity - infinity

  assert(x = y)
  assert(x =/= z)
  assert(x < z)
  assert(x <= z)
  assert(z > x)
  assert(z >= x)
  assert(x CMP z, LessThan)
  assert(x MIN z, x)
  assert(x MAX z, z)
  assert((x MIN NaN).isNaN, true)
  assert((x MAX NaN).isNaN, true)
  assert(-x, narrow(-14.0))
  assert(x + y, sum)
  assert(x - y, zero)
  assert(x DOT y, z)
  assert(x TIMES y, z)
  assert(z, mul)
  assert(z / x, x)

  assert(SQRT z, x)
  assert(x PLUS_UP y, sum)
  assert(x MINUS_UP y, zero)
  assert(x DOT_UP y, mul)
  assert(x SLASH_UP y, one)
  assert(SQRT_UP z, x)
  assert(x PLUS_DOWN y, sum)
  assert(x MINUS_DOWN y, zero)
  assert(x DOT_DOWN y, mul)
  assert(x SLASH_DOWN y, one)
  assert(SQRT_DOWN z, x)
  assert(|x|, x)
  assert(|-x|, x)
  assert(x^two, mul)
  assert(floor v, four)
  assert(|\ v /|, four)
  assert(ceiling v, five)
  assert(|/ v \|, five)
  assert(truncate v, four)
  assert(floor w, nfive)
  assert(|\ w /|, nfive)
  assert(ceiling w, nfour)
  assert(|/ w \|, nfour)
  assert(truncate w, nfour)
  assert(x.isNaN, false)
  assert(x.isInfinite, false)
  assert(infinity.isInfinite, true)
  assert(x.isNumber, true)
  assert(x.isFinite, true)
  assert(infinity.isFinite, false)
  assert(Just(v), Just(v))
  assert(Just(z), Just(z))
  (* If we do not give explicit type instantiation below, it fails... *)
  assert(x.check, Just[\RR32\](x))
  assert(infinity.check, Nothing[\RR32\])
  assert(NaN.check, Nothing[\RR32\])

  assert(x.check_star, Just[\RR32\](x))
  assert(infinity.check_star, Just[\RR32\](infinity))
  assert(NaN.check_star, Nothing[\RR32\])

  (* We want to implement hexadecimal literals. *)
  assert((x / x).rawBits, 1065353216)
  assert(x MINNUM z, x)
  assert(x MAXNUM z, z)
  assert(x MINNUM NaN, x)
  assert(x MAXNUM NaN, x)
end

end
import List.{...}
import Set.{...}
import Map.{...}

object Properties extends GenericProperties
    (* Tests a non-generic property. *)
    propAssociativeAddition(a:ZZ32, b:ZZ32, c:ZZ32): Boolean =
        ((a DOTPLUS b) DOTPLUS c) = (a DOTPLUS (b DOTPLUS c))

    (* Tests a polymorphic property and its desugared form. *)
    (* XXX RR32 + RR64 doesn't work correctly! *)
    propCommutativeAddition(a:Number, b:Number): Boolean =
        (*)a + b = b + a
        asFloat(a) + asFloat(b) = asFloat(b) + asFloat(a)
    propCommutativeAddition'[\A extends Number, B extends Number\](a:A, b:B): Boolean =
        (*)a + b = b + a
        asFloat(a) + asFloat(b) = asFloat(b) + asFloat(a)

    (* Tests several variants of same property. *)
    propDoubleReversal[\T\](g:Generator[\T\]): Boolean =
        (list g.reverse.reverse = list g)
    propDoubleReversalList[\T\](g:List[\T\]): Boolean =
        (list g.reverse.reverse = list g)
    propDoubleReversalSet[\T\](g:Set[\T\]): Boolean =
        (list g.reverse.reverse = list g)
    propDoubleReversalMap[\K,V\](g:Map[\K,V\]): Boolean =
        (list g.reverse.reverse = list g)

    (* Specific properties for `Map`. *)
    propMapSizeInvariant1[\Key,Val\](map:Map[\Key,Val\], k:Key, v:Val): Boolean =
        (0 <= |map.add(k,v)| - |map| <= 1)
        div = num GCD den    (*) so we have unique representation for every equivalent `QQ`
        genZZ.perturb(den DIV div, genZZ.perturb(num DIV div, g))
    end
end

object genRR32 extends Gen[\RR32\]
    getter asString(): String = "genRR32"

    generate(c:TestContext): RR32 = do
        x = c.random()
        narrow(genZZ32.generate(c) (x / 4294967296.0 (* 2.0^32 *)))
    end

    perturb(obj:RR32, g:AnySeededRandomGen): AnySeededRandomGen =
        genZZ32.perturb(obj.rawBits, g)
end

object genRR32small extends Gen[\RR32\]
    getter asString(): String = "genRR32small"
    generate(c:TestContext): RR32 =
        narrow(c.random() / 2147483648.0 (* 2.0^31 *) - 0.5)
    perturb(obj:RR32, g:AnySeededRandomGen): AnySeededRandomGen =
        genZZ32.perturb(obj.rawBits, g)
end

    opr MAX(self, other:RR64): RR64 = if self >= other then self elif other >= self then other elif self.isNaN then self else other end
    opr MINNUM(self, other:RR64): RR64 = if self <= other then self elif other <= self then other elif self.isNaN then other else self end
    opr MAXNUM(self, other:RR64): RR64 = if self >= other then self elif other >= self then other elif self.isNaN then other else self end
    opr MINNUMMAX(self, other:RR64): (RR64, RR64) = if self <= other then (self, other) elif other <= self then (other, self) elif other.isNaN then (self, other) else (other, self) end
    opr MINMAXNUM(self, other:RR64): (RR64, RR64) = if self <= other then (self, other) elif other <= self then (other, self) elif self.isNaN then (self, other) else (other, self) end
    opr ^(self, other:RR64): RR64 = jDoublePow(self,other)
    opr ^(self, other:ZZ32): RR64 =
        if other > 2 then
            mid = other DIV 2
            if (mid + mid) = other then
                (self self)^mid
            else

        elif other = 2 then self self
        elif other = 1 then self
        elif other = 0 then 1.0
        elif other = -other then

          1.0 / (self^(-(other DIV 2)))^2

        else (* other < 0 then *) 1.0 / (self^(-other))

\chapter{Numbers}
\chaplabel{lib:numbers-basic}


\section{Rational Numbers}
\seclabel{basic-rationals}

The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} (\STR{QQ}) encompasses all finite rational numbers,
the results of dividing any integer by any nonzero integer,
and three more elements:
\EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty} (written \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0}),
the results of dividing a positive or a negative integer by zero,
and the indefinite rational (written \EXP{0/0}), which is used as the result
of dividing zero by zero or of adding \EXP{-\infty} to \EXP{+\infty}.

The number types of this chapter are
the integer types \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} (\secref{basic-integers}),
the rational type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}},
and the floating-point type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (\STR{RR64}).
They are siblings under the trait \TYP{Number}:
each is a subtype of \TYP{Number}, and none is a subtype of another.
Some conversions between them are coercions (\chapref{conversions-coercions}),
each declared by the type converted to;
since coercions do not chain (\secref{coercion}), each pair is declared.
Those among the integer types are given in \secref{basic-integers};
the others are these:

\begin{tabbing}
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} (\STR{QQ}) coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}.
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (\STR{RR64}) coerces from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and from integer numerals (\secref{literals}).
\end{tabbing}

Every other conversion between number types is written explicitly;
in particular, a conversion into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}
is explicit, written \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} with the method that \library\ declare on \TYP{Number}.

It is often desirable to know that a value lies in a subset of its type,
such as the positive values, the nonzero values, or the finite values.
Such subsets are not types of their own: a program tests a value at run time,
with the comparison operators for its sign and, for a floating-point value,
with the two checks that \library\ declare on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}:
%getter check(): Maybe[\RR64\]
%getter check_star(): Maybe[\RR64\]
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{getter}\:\VAR{check}()\COLON \TYP{Maybe}\llbracket\mathbb{R}64\rrbracket\)\\
\(\KWD{getter}\:\VAR{check}^*()\COLON \TYP{Maybe}\llbracket\mathbb{R}64\rrbracket\)
\end{Fortress}
The getter \VAR{check} returns \EXP{\TYP{Just}(x)} for a finite value \VAR{x}
and \TYP{Nothing} otherwise;
the getter \EXP{\VAR{check}^*} returns \EXP{\TYP{Just}(x)} for a value \VAR{x}
that is not a NaN and \TYP{Nothing} otherwise.

Here we present the trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and its methods.
Because \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} holds \EXP{0/0}, which is unordered with respect to every
rational value, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is neither totally ordered nor a field.
The original design of the rational types, in which \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
seventeen refined rational types are instantiations of one trait, is kept as a
superseded design in \secref{advanced-rationals}.

\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
\seclabel{revival-changes}
\sloppy

This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
open disagreement.
Each changed passage carries a box headed
``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.

Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
would require.
The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
there.
The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
Fortress~1.0 release.
The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
new one, is in the revival's decision records,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
and, for the number chapters,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
in the same repository.

Every change below follows from one decision of the revival, taken on
24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}: the compiled type checker keeps
the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
stated, and the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
satisfy it.
The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
\secref{revival-routec}.

......
\subsection{The number types}
\seclabel{revival-numbers}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{basic-rationals}; \secref{basic-integers}.
\item[Change] The eighteen rational types and the twelve integer types of the
original, with \EXP{\mathbb{N}} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}^*}, each a subtype of others,
are replaced by seven number types \library\ declare: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}},
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{N}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, siblings under \TYP{Number}, with the
coercions the library declares: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}; \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}; \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}
from the four fixed-size types; \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} from the five integer types;
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and from integer numerals.
Every other conversion between them is explicit, the one into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} written \EXP{\VAR{asFloat}(x)} with the method the library declares on \TYP{Number}.
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} includes \EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty} and \EXP{0/0}; the integer
types hold no infinite value.
A subset such as the positive values is tested at run time, and the two checks
the library declares, \VAR{check} and \EXP{\VAR{check}^*} on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64},
returning \EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket\mathbb{R}64\rrbracket}, are stated.
The sentences that the type system tracks the refined types through arithmetic
are removed, and so are the sentences that \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a field and totally
ordered and that \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*} is not a ring; \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, which holds
\EXP{0/0}, is stated to be neither totally ordered nor a field.
\item[Rationale] Route~A makes the library's numeric types siblings under
\TYP{Number}, each with its own algebra, a wider type converting a narrower one
by coercion, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} inside \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} by coercion.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that the refined types become the
library's own run-time checks, which return a \TYP{Maybe}, and that their
original design is kept as a superseded design (\secref{revival-superseded});
and that a conversion between number types is a coercion where it is exact and
stays explicit where it can lose precision, the coercion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} being declared from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the numerals only.
\Library\ never declared the refined types, and the trait that defines them is
refused by instantiation exclusion (\secref{revival-rule}).
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} holds the values that \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}
added, as the library's rational type does, and as \chapref{operators} already
says: ``For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.''
The type that holds \EXP{0/0} is ``neither totally ordered nor a field'' in the
original's own words.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) keeps the statement that the
numeric types are mutually exclusive (\secref{types-libraries}).
\item[Effect] A program names \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} where it named a
refined type, and tests a sign or finiteness at run time.
A generic call over two different integer types writes its static
argument until the rule that infers the narrowest type both coerce into is
written into \chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation.
The conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, though exact,
stays explicit, since the decision names only \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and the
numerals.
The library's \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} stays below \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, as before, a
value object that adds no instantiation of its own.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex},

\begin{quote}
The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} (\STR{QQ}) encompasses all finite rational numbers,
the results of dividing any integer by any nonzero integer.
The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} with
two extra elements, \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}.
The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} with
one additional element, the indefinite rational (written \EXP{0/0}), which is used as the result
of dividing zero by zero or of adding \EXP{-\infty} to \EXP{+\infty}.

Often it is desirable to indicate that a variable ranges over only a subset of
the rationals, such as only positive values or only nonnegative values or only
nonzero values.
Unfortunately, traditional notations such as \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^+} are not used consistently
in the literature; one author may use \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^+} to mean the set of strictly positive rationals
and another may use it to mean the set of nonnegative rationals.
Fortress therefore uses a notation that is novel but unambiguous:

\begin{tabbing}
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} (\STR{QQ}) is the set of rationals
(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}LT}) is the set of strictly negative rationals
(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\leq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}LE}) is the set of nonpositive rationals, that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<} \cup \{0\}}
(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{\leq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}GE}) is the set of nonnegative rationals, that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>} \cup \{0\}}
(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{\geq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}).
\\
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}GT}) is the set of strictly positive rationals
(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}}).

Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}

argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
type by the expected type; a type parameter that
is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
which every one of them converts, and otherwise the union of their types; every
argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
inferred again without it when its result then converts.
A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
infers.
The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
box.
The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
\chapref{type-inference}.
\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule
written into this chapter; on 27~September 2026 that the compiled type checker
infers static arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call
written as \EXP{f(x)}, with a retry without it so that a coercion of the result
still applies, and that the chapter is written with it; and on 28~September
2026 that a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration
runs when one is applicable without it, the declaration chosen being then
instantiated by that rule, that a numeral whose conversions tie is read as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral does.
\chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and \secref{dotted-method-calls}
said that static arguments are inferred as \chapref{type-inference} describes,
and it described nothing; once the compiled type checker infers them by a rule
the text does not state, the text and the implementation disagree, so the
chapter states the rule that the checker builds, and no more.
The order, a declaration chosen and then instantiated, is that of
\secref{resolving-coercion}, read on the parameter types that declarations
declare, as the type group's paper of 2011 reads a declaration with static
parameters: it ``is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its
instances is'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 396--397, in the
revival's repository).

a numeral the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and

declarations that a numeral left tied, and not always the same one (row~391 of
the revival's gap ledger).

The compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
so an \KWD{int} parameter is read as a \KWD{nat} parameter is; on the Java

type (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines

\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md}

\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
\seclabel{revival-notrevised}

No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
contradict is known to be unrevised.
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-inference}); the passages that chapter leaves unrevised are the
sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} by which static parameters are inferred
before the applicability of a declaration is checked and before declarations
are compared, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the rule of
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} on a naked type parameter of bound \TYP{Any},
which are to be revised with the overloading chapters. The result of an integer raised to a negative power is not yet given (\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-integers}).
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
\begin{quote}
The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
library's nested tower today.
They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
behind it.
Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
\seclabel{revival-routec}

The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
instantiations when they form a chain.
The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
type checker and code generator.
Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
types.
Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
no chain contains.
Under route~C the numeric chapters could have kept the nesting of their
widths, and their original text, quoted in \secref{revival-numbers} and the
entries after it and kept in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's
for that nesting; route~C rescues neither the refined number types nor
\TYP{RationalQuantity} (\secref{revival-numbers}).
The record of the experiment is
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
revival's repository.

The paragraph above adds the property.
It is the rule the type group named \emph{multiple instantiation exclusion}
(Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele,
``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and
Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011), which the compiled type checker enforces
for type arguments and numerals, not yet in every case (\secref{revival-rule} states its coverage),

under its shorter name.}

\subsection{Object Trait Types}
\seclabel{object-traits}

An object trait type is a trait type defined by an object declaration.
Object declarations do not include \KWD{excludes} clauses,
but an object trait type cannot be extended.
Thus, an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype.

\section{Object Expression Types}
\seclabel{object-exp-types}

An object expression type is defined by an object expression
(described in \secref{object-expr})
and the program location of the object expression.
Every evaluation of a given object expression has the same
object expression type.  Two object expressions at different program locations
have different object expression types.

Like trait types,
an object expression type is a subtype of all trait types
that appear in the \KWD{extends} clause of its definition,
as well as the type \TYP{Any}.

Like object trait types,
an object expression type excludes any type that is not its supertype.

For example, a coercion may occur in a variable definition when the
declared type of the variable is \VAR{U} and the type of the expression on
the right-hand side is a subtype of \VAR{T}.


The expression contexts where a coercion can occur are:
\begin{itemize}
\item the right-hand sides of variable and field declarations where the
  left-hand sides have declared types
\item arguments to functionals and constructors where the corresponding
  parameters have declared types
\item body expressions of functionals and constructors where the return
  types are declared
\item the right-hand sides of test and property declarations
\item expressions in contracts

The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
\begin{itemize}
\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
type of the instance.
\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
expected type as well.
\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
the type parameter permit.
For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
(\secref{basic-integers}).
Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
the union of the types of those arguments (\secref{internal-types}), if its
bounds permit that, and none of those arguments is converted.

is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it

parameter of a declaration without static parameters.

trait Equality[\T extends Equality[\T\]\]
    opr =(self, other:T): Boolean = self SEQV other
end

(** Total ordering *)

object LexicographicPartialReduction
        extends { MonoidReduction[\Comparison\],
                  ReductionWithZeroes[\Comparison, Comparison\] }
    getter asString():String = "Lexicographic reduction on partial order"
    empty(): Comparison = EqualTo
    join(a:Comparison, b:Comparison):Comparison = a LEXICO b
    isZero(_:Unordered): Boolean = true
trait StandardMin[\T extends StandardMin[\T\]\]
    opr MIN(self, other:T): T
end

(** %StandardMax% is a MAX operator; most types that implement %MAX%
    will implement a corresponding total order.  It's a separate type
    to account for the existence of floating point numbers, for which
    NaN counts as a bottom that is less than anything else but doesn't
    actually participate in the standard total ordering.  It is
    otherwise the case that %a MAX b = a% when %a <= b% and that
    %a MAX b = b MAX a%. **)
trait StandardMax[\T extends StandardMax[\T\]\]
    opr MAX(self, other:T): T
end

(** %StandardMinMax% combines MIN and MAX operators, and provides a
    combined MINMAX operator.  This operator returns both its
    arguments; if equality is possible, self should be the leftmost
    result.  This effectively means that %(a MINMAX b)% stably sorts
    %a% and %b%.  In addition, %a MINMAX b = (a MIN b, a MAX b)% must
    always hold. **)

trait StandardMinMax[\T extends StandardMinMax[\T\]\]
        extends { StandardMin[\T\], StandardMax[\T\] }
    opr MINMAX(self, other:T): (T,T)
    opr MIN(self, other:T): T = do (r,_) = self MINMAX other; r end
    opr MAX(self, other:T): T = do (_,r) = self MINMAX other; r end
end

(** StandardTotalOrder is the usual total order using <,>,<=,>=,=, and
    CMP.  Most values that define a comparison should do so using
    this.  Minimal complete definition: either CMP or < (it's
    advisable to define = in the latter case).  As noted above, %MIN%
    and %MAX% respect the total order and are defined in the obvious
    way. **)
trait StandardTotalOrder[\T extends StandardTotalOrder[\T\]\]
        extends { StandardPartialOrder[\T\], StandardMinMax[\T\] }
    opr CMP(self, other:T): TotalComparison =
        if self < other then LessThan
        elif other < self then GreaterThan
        else EqualTo
        end
    opr >=(self, other:T): Boolean = NOT (self < other)
    opr <=(self, other:T): Boolean = NOT (other < self)
    opr MIN(self, other:T): T = if other < self then other else self end
    opr MAX(self, other:T): T = if other < self then self else other end
    opr MINMAX(self, other:T): (T,T) =
        if other < self then (other, self) else (self, other) end
end

(** Assertion *)
assert(flag:Boolean): () =
    if NOT flag then
        fail("Assertion failed!")
    end

assert(flag: Boolean, failMsg: String): () =
    if NOT flag then
        fail(failMsg)
    end

assert(x:Any, y:Any, failMsg: Any...): () =
    if x =/= y then
        msg = x.asDebugString " =/= " y.asDebugString "; " (BIG || failMsg)  (* use || here instead of loose juxt *)
        fail(msg)
    end

deny(flag:Boolean): () = assert(NOT flag)

deny(flag: Boolean, failMsg: String): () = assert(NOT flag, failMsg)

deny(x:Any, y:Any, failMsg: Any...): () =
    if x = y then
        msg = x.asDebugString " = " y.asDebugString "; " (BIG || failMsg)
        fail(msg)
    end

shouldRaise⟦Ex extends Exception⟧ (expr: ()→()): () = do
    try
        expr()
        throw ForbiddenException
    catch x
        Ex => assert(true) (* This is what we hope for *)
    forbid Exception
    end
end

* Numeric hierarchy
************************************************************)

trait AnyAdditiveGroup end

(** Additive group making use of +.  Must define + and either unary or binary -. **)
trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
    getter zero(): T = self - self
    opr +(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self, other: T): T = self + (-other)
    opr -(self) : T = self.zero - self
end

component RR32SiblingRungV
export Executable

(*) explorations/compile-ladder/rung-rr32-sibling/REPORT.md

shownV(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    RR32 => v.asString || " : RR32"
    RR64 => v.asString || " : RR64"
    else => v.asString || " : other"
  end

floatKindV(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    RR64 => "an RR64"
    RR32 => "an RR32"
    else => "other"
  end

r64V(x: RR64): String = shownV(x)

pairV[\T extends Number\](x: T, y: T): String = shownV(x) ", " shownV(y)

run() = do
    a: RR32 = narrow(1.5)
    b: RR32 = narrow(2.5)
    f: RR64 = asFloat(2.5)
    g: RR64 = asFloat(1.5)
    z: ZZ32 = 2

    assert(floatKindV(a), "an RR32", "types-vals-vars.tex:536: an RR32 is not an RR64")
    assert(floatKindV(f), "an RR64", "types-vals-vars.tex:536: control, an RR64 is an RR64")

    assert(shownV(a + b), "4.0 : RR32", "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: RR32 + RR32 by RR32's own +")
    assert(shownV(a - b), "-1.0 : RR32", "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: RR32 - RR32 by RR32's own -")
    assert(shownV(-a), "-1.5 : RR32", "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: - RR32 by RR32's own -")
    assert(shownV(a b), "3.75 : RR32", "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: RR32 RR32 by RR32's own juxtaposition")
    assert(shownV(a / b), "0.6 : RR32", "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: RR32 / RR32 by RR32's own /")
    assert(shownV(SQRT a), "1.2247449 : RR32", "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: SQRT RR32 by RR32's own SQRT")
    assert(shownV(a^2), "2.25 : RR32", "FortressLibrary.fss:355-356: MultiplicativeRing[\\RR32\\]'s ^ answers an RR32")
    assert(shownV(a MIN b), "1.5 : RR32", "POSITIONS.md:134, decision 2: RR32's own MIN")
    assert(shownV(a MAX b), "2.5 : RR32", "POSITIONS.md:134, decision 2: RR32's own MAX")
    (lo, hi) = a MINMAX b
    assert(shownV(lo) ", " shownV(hi), "1.5 : RR32, 2.5 : RR32", "POSITIONS.md:134, decision 2: RR32's own MINMAX")

    assert(shownV(a + f), "4.0 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 + RR64 by RR64's + after the coercion")
    assert(shownV(f + a), "4.0 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR64 + RR32 by RR64's + after the coercion")
    assert(shownV(a + 2.5), "4.0 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 + a float numeral by RR64's +")
    assert(shownV(2.5 + a), "4.0 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: a float numeral + RR32 by RR64's +")
    assert(shownV(a + z), "3.5 : RR64", "numbers.tex:43, conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 + ZZ32 by RR64's +")
    assert(shownV(a + 2), "3.5 : RR64", "numbers.tex:43, conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 + an integer numeral by RR64's +")
    assert(shownV(a MIN f), "1.5 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 MIN RR64 by RR64's MIN")
    assert(shownV(a MAX 2.5), "2.5 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 MAX a float numeral by RR64's MAX")
    (lo2, hi2) = a MINMAX f
    assert(shownV(lo2) ", " shownV(hi2), "1.5 : RR64, 2.5 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 MINMAX RR64 by RR64's MINMAX")

    x: RR64 = a
    assert(shownV(x), "1.5 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:115-117: an RR32 bound to an RR64 variable converts")
    assert(r64V(a), "1.5 : RR64", "conversions-coercions.tex:115-119: an RR32 passed to an RR64 parameter converts")
    assert(pairV(a, f), "1.5 : RR64, 2.5 : RR64", "inference.tex:82-92: T is RR64 for an RR32 and an RR64")
    assert(pairV(a, b), "1.5 : RR32, 2.5 : RR32", "inference.tex:82-92: control, T is RR32 for two RR32 arguments")

    assert(a = g, "FortressLibrary.fsi:284-288: RR32 = RR64 compares after asFloat")
    assert(g = a, "FortressLibrary.fsi:284-288: RR64 = RR32 compares after asFloat")
    assert(a = 1.5, "FortressLibrary.fsi:284-288: RR32 = a float numeral compares after asFloat")
    deny(a = b, "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: RR32 = RR32 by RR32's own =")
    assert(a < f, "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 < RR64 by RR64's < after the coercion")
    assert(a < 2.5, "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 < a float numeral by RR64's <")
    deny(2.5 < a, "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: a float numeral < RR32 by RR64's <")
    assert(a CMP f, LessThan, "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR32 CMP RR64 by RR64's CMP")
    assert(f CMP a, GreaterThan, "conversions-coercions.tex:909-912: RR64 CMP RR32 by RR64's CMP")
    assert(a CMP b, LessThan, "conversions-coercions.tex:904-908: RR32 CMP RR32 by RR32's own CMP")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

mkdir -p "$SCRATCH/classes" "$SCRATCH/caches" "$(dirname "$OUT")" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
if [ -z "$CP" ] ; then echo "checker-count: no classpath from bin/fortress_classpath" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi

# 1. build the driver and the instrumented checker against the tree's own classpath

# The integer rules, row 394's example and the rational type's algebra in the specification: the decision record

Climb batch 6.5, rung P (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.5.md`, section 3, P). This record gives the full reasoning of the rung's four Appendix I entries: "Shifts and narrowing on the integer types" (`\secref{revival-shifts}`), "The greatest common divisor and the least common multiple" (`revival-gcd`), "The example of coercion resolution" (`revival-coercion-example`) and "The algebra of the rational trait" (`revival-rational-algebra`), `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1340-1545`; the appendix points here from the first of them (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1382`). Line numbers are on this rung's tree unless they say the base (`b797d8037`) or the Working Draft of February 2011 (`Specification-1.0-frozen/`).

## 1. Why the specification changes

Pavol's requirement of 2026-09-24: "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation" (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-24, a requirement on the plan). Climb batches 3.5 and 4 built integer rules that no specification text states (`explorations/reviews/batch-3.5-4-conformance.md`, "Batch 3.5 as a whole" and finding 3). The coercion chapter's own example contradicts its definition (ledger row 394). The rational type's listing names less algebra than the library declares (`explorations/reviews/batch-6-conformance.md`, smaller findings). Every change takes the S1 form (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, S1): the text edited in place, a `\revision` callout at each changed passage, an Appendix I entry quoting the Working Draft of February 2011 by path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the first of the batch-5 answers), and this record.

## 2. The rules, their decisions, and what runs them

Each rule below is stated once in the specification. "Walk" is the interpreter, "compiled" the bytecode path with its own prelude (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`) until the switch-over.

| rule | decision | walk | compiled |
|---|---|---|---|
| `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on a fixed width `n`: for `k >= 0`, `x RSHIFT k` is `floor(x/2^k)` and `x LSHIFT k` is `x 2^k` reduced into the type modulo `2^n`; so a count at or beyond the width gives `0`, or for a right shift the replicated sign; a negative count shifts the other way | POSITIONS 2026-09-22, ledger row 335 | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:182-193`, `Long.java:194-206`, `NN32.java:188-200`, `UnsignedLong.java:189-201` | `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:354-362`, `simpleLongArith.java:323-331`, bound at `CompilerBuiltin.fss:647-648`, `:736-737`; `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` only |
| the count of any integer type, read by its value (an `NN64` count of `2^63` or more is beyond the width) | POSITIONS 2026-09-24, ledger rows 380 and 381 | `Int.shiftCount`, `Int.java:263-274`; `ZZ32`'s pair declared `b:AnyIntegral`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:542-543` | a count of the receiver's own type only (row 381, closes at the switch-over) |
| on `ZZ`, `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` are `shift(x,k)` and `shift(x,-k)`; `shift` is exact at any count; a result too large for the implementation throws `IntegerOverflow` | POSITIONS 2026-09-22, ledger row 335 | `BigNum.java:228-254` (`LShift`, `RShift`, `shiftLeft`), `shift` bound to `BigNum$LShift`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:989-990` | no `LSHIFT` or `shift` on `ZZ` (row 383); its `<<<` refuses the same shifts, `simpleArbitraryPrecisionArith.java:93-102` |
| `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits, signed and unsigned | POSITIONS 2026-09-22, ledger row 346; 2026-09-24, climb batch 3.5 (the signed `narrow` too) | `Long$FromLong`, `Long.java:250-254`; `UnsignedLong$FromLong`, `UnsignedLong.java:245-249`; `BigNum$ToZZ32`, `BigNum.java:286-290` | `ZZ64.narrow`, `NN64.narrow`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`, `:879`; no `narrow` on `ZZ` |
| `GCD` and `LCM` nonnegative; for an argument `0` (`GCD`) or `1` (`LCM`) the result is the other argument's absolute value; `(m GCD n)(m LCM n) = abs(m n)` | POSITIONS 2026-09-22, ledger row 334 | `Int.java:136-150`, `:276-326`; `Long.java:150-162`; `BigNum.java:176-192` | `CompilerBuiltin.fss:609-623`, `:694-708` |
| a `GCD` or `LCM` that the fixed-size type cannot hold throws `IntegerOverflow` | POSITIONS 2026-09-22, ledger row 334; the specification's general sentence, `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`; POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the fifth batch-5 answer (the unsigned types by the same rule) | `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` as above; `NN32`'s and `NN64`'s `LCM` do not yet (climb batch 6.5b, rung E) | `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` as above; `NN32`, `NN64` declare neither |

Measured: the gated tests `ProjectFortress/tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss` (walk) and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/IntSemanticsRungB.fss`, `ProjectFortress/library_tests/IntegralOpsRungN.fss`, `ProjectFortress/library_tests/IntConversionsRungW.fss` (compiled) assert most of the table; the rest is measured by this rung's probes, `probes/rules/RulesWalk.walk.txt` (19 cases, all as the text says: `ZZ`'s `narrow`, `NN32` at and beyond the width, `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on `ZZ` as `shift`, their overflow, `ZZ` and `NN32` counts on a `ZZ32`) and `probes/rules/RulesCompiled.compiled.txt` (the operator overview's two examples, `(2^31-1) LCM 2` and `-2^31 GCD 0`, both `IntegerOverflow`; `0 GCD -4 = 4`, `1 LCM -5 = 5`).

The reasons behind the rules, from the decisions: the design principle of 2026-09-22, "we should use Java or JVM defaults where it makes sense, but we shouldn't be shy to correct the mistakes of JVM when seen through the lens of high performance and mathematical precision language", with hardware behaviour given its own spelling; on the shifts, that every peer language lets shifted-out bits fall because a shift is a bit operation, with the arithmetic `shift` kept exact on `ZZ`; for a count at or beyond the width, the rule the team's interpreter has followed since `b451f5506` (2007-06-26) and that `ProjectFortress/tests/BitTwiddle.fss:33`, `:36`, `:39`, `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:30`, `:32`, `:135`, `:137` and `ProjectFortress/tests/QuickCheckTest.fss:97-103` assert (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-integral-ops/shift-history.md`, section 2); for `narrow`, Steele's boundary test of 2008-07-21, `ProjectFortress/tests/UnsignedTest.fss:210-211`; for `GCD` and `LCM`, the chapter's own "The result is always nonnegative" and the `NN` of its suppressed declarations (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:518-519`).

## 3. The places

The list (`probes/list/list.txt`) names every passage of `Specification/` outside `library/apis/` that names a shift, `narrow`, `GCD`, `LCM`, an integer overflow or the fixed-width types' operators, and what becomes of each. The rung revises these:
- `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:39-66`, two paragraphs after "every other conversion between integer types is written explicitly" (`:36-37`), which named no conversion: `narrow`, then `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` on the five types; callout `:63-66`.
- `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:725-730`, the entry of `shift`: exactness, overflow, `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on `ZZ`; callout `:729-730`.
- `Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:541-568`, the entry of `GCD` and `LCM`: the absolute value, `abs(m n)`; callout `:562-568`.
- `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:262-270`, "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators": the sign and the overflow, two examples; callout `:269-270`.
- `Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:341-344`, "Logical Operators": `LSHIFT` and `RSHIFT` named beside the bitwise operators; callout `:343-344`.
- `Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:556-597`, row 394's example.
- `Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:92-94`, `:145-147`, `:217-224`, the rational listing's header and one sentence.

## 4. Decisions taken inside the rung

1. **The integer rules go in the integer chapter's opening, not in the `ZZ` listing and not in api comments.** The opening introduces the fixed-size types and ends on the explicit conversions; the rules concern all five types, where the listing and its method entries present `ZZ` alone. Rejected: (a) listing entries for `LSHIFT`, `RSHIFT` and `narrow` on `ZZ`, which would state the rules for `ZZ` only and leave the fixed widths, the types they matter for, undescribed; (b) comments on `Integral`'s shift pair and the `narrow` declarations in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, which batch 3.5 and 4's review offered, which Part IV renders, and which this rung may not edit (a library line other than the scalar comments is a stop); the prose chapters are the standard (FACTS.md, "Citing Specification/library/apis/*.tex as an independent standard is circular"); (c) a new section on the fixed-size types, heavier than two paragraphs for the same content.
2. **The operator overview gets two sentences on `GCD`/`LCM` and one on the shifts.** It is the passage that describes the integer operators for every integer type, and its `GCD` subsection is in the list; without the shift sentence its list of bitwise operators omits two the library declares. Rejected: leaving the overview unchanged, which keeps the overview silent on the one question of the fixed widths the revised integer chapter cannot answer for `GCD` and `LCM` (the chapter's entry is on `ZZ`, which never overflows).

#!/bin/bash
# comp.sh <dir-of-probe> <Name> [shadow-classes-dir]: compile <dir>/<Name>.fss with the bytecode compiler in the
# compiler's world into a private cache seeded from tmp/libcache, run it, and capture <dir>/<Name>.comp.txt
# (the shape of explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement/comp.sh, with env-noclean.sh and a shadow);
# LIBCACHE overrides the seed cache and LABEL the capture's suffix (default comp).
D="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
source "$D/env-noclean.sh"
JAVA_FLAGS="$JAVA_FLAGS ${EXTRA_FLAGS:-}"
P=$(cd "${1:?usage}" && pwd); N=${2:?usage}; SH=${3:-}
L="${LIBCACHE:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/libcache}"
C="$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/cache-comp-$N-${LABEL:-comp}"
rm -rf "$C"; cp -r "$L" "$C"; mkdir -p "$C/tmp"
CP=$("$FORTRESS_HOME/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1)
[ -n "$SH" ] && CP="$SH:$CP"
cd "$P"
{
  echo "# comp.sh $N $(date -u +%FT%TZ); tree $(git -C "$FORTRESS_HOME" rev-parse --short HEAD); nproc=$(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | sed 's/.*: //') MHz; load $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | grep -m1 version); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; shadow ${SH:-none}"
  echo "## fortress compile $N.fss (private cache, compiler's world)"
  timeout -k 10 1800 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$C -Djava.io.tmpdir=$C/tmp -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile "$N.fss" 2>&1
  echo "compile rc=$?"
  echo "## run"
  timeout -k 10 600 java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches="$C" -cp "$C/bytecode_cache:$C/bytecode_cache/*:$C/nativewrapper_cache:$CP" com.sun.fortress.runtimeSystem.MainWrapper "$N" 2>&1
  echo "run rc=$?"
} > "$P/$N.${LABEL:-comp}.txt" 2>&1
cat "$P/$N.${LABEL:-comp}.txt"
